Sociologists study how global online communities form, how international markets and outsourcing affect inequality, and how global culture influences local traditions. At the same time, the chapter shows that sociology remains grounded in concrete social issues: it helps explain inequality, discrimination, family change, and public policy debates. The research of Kenneth and Mamie Clark, for example, influenced the Supreme Court’s Brown v. Board of Education decision by showing the harmful effects of segregation on children. More broadly, sociology contributes to social reform in areas such as workplace equality, mental health, disability access, Indigenous rights, and prison reform.

Studying sociology is valuable because it helps people understand how society shapes individual lives, see the world from others’ perspectives, question simple explanations, and think critically about social problems. It also provides transferable skills useful in many jobs, including research, data analysis, communication, and understanding organizations and diverse populations. Sociology graduates work in government, social services, counseling, health, marketing, human resources, education, law, journalism, and criminal justice. Finally, sociology is useful for analyzing modern issues such as the long-term consequences of social media behavior, including how institutions like colleges and employers interpret online speech and how research can inform fair policies and practices.

This chapter explains how sociologists understand societies, social theory, and everyday reality as socially created.

Societies are groups of people sharing a common community, culture, and often political authority. Sociologist Gerhard Lenski classified societies by their level of technology, from preindustrial to industrial to postindustrial. In preindustrial societies, life depends heavily on the environment and local resources. Hunter-gatherer societies are nomadic and rely on hunting and foraging; pastoral societies domesticate animals and remain mobile; horticultural societies cultivate crops and can settle permanently; agricultural societies use advanced farming tools and surplus production, leading to towns, trade, specialization, class divisions, and greater inequality. Feudal societies later developed around land ownership, with lords, vassals, and peasants bound by protection and labor obligations.

Industrial societies emerged with the Industrial Revolution, when steam power and mechanization transformed production, agriculture, transportation, and daily life. Factories, urbanization, wage labor, social mobility, labor conflict, and labor unions became central features. Industrialization also helped shape many modern social ideas, including standardized time, childhood, and family roles. Postindustrial or information societies are based less on manufacturing and more on information, services, and digital technology. In these societies, education and technical skills become major sources of power and inequality.

The chapter also shows that technology can have very different social effects. It can damage environments and disrupt communities, but it can also improve life and support local development, as seen in solar projects that bring electricity and autonomy to rural villages.

Three major sociological perspectives help explain society. Émile Durkheim’s functionalism views society as an interconnected system whose parts work together to maintain stability. He introduced the ideas of the collective conscience, social integration, social facts, mechanical solidarity in small traditional societies, organic solidarity in complex modern societies, and anomie, or normlessness during periods of social disruption. Durkheim believed even deviance serves a social function by reinforcing moral boundaries.

Karl Marx’s conflict theory sees society as shaped by economic structure and class struggle. He argued that the economic base determines the cultural and institutional superstructure. In capitalism, the bourgeoisie own the means of production while the proletariat sell their labor, creating exploitation and conflict. Marx described alienation as the worker’s separation from the product of labor, the labor process, other people, and even the self. He also introduced false consciousness, in which workers accept ideas that serve the dominant class, and class consciousness, in which workers recognize their common interests and can pursue social change.

Max Weber emphasized class, status, power, rationalization, and the effects of modern bureaucracy. He argued that modern society becomes increasingly rationalized, prioritizing efficiency, rules, and calculation over tradition and morality. This creates an “iron cage” that can trap individuals in bureaucratic systems and produce a sense of disenchantment. Weber also explained the Protestant work ethic, arguing that Calvinist ideas about predestination encouraged disciplined work and success, helping lay the cultural foundations of capitalism.

The final section explains that reality itself is socially constructed. Berger and Luckmann argued that repeated actions become habitualized and then institutionalized, so society appears natural even though it is created through human interaction. Thomas’s theorem states that if people define situations as real, they become real in their consequences. This idea helps explain self-fulfilling prophecies, where beliefs can make themselves come true. Symbolic interactionists focus on how people use symbols, language, and gestures to create meaning in daily life.

People also move through social life by taking on roles linked to statuses. Some statuses are ascribed, while others are achieved. A person may experience role strain when one role is too demanding and role conflict when different roles clash. Erving Goffman’s dramaturgy compares social life to theater: people perform roles, manage impressions, and use setting and props to influence how others see them. Charles Cooley’s looking-glass self adds that our self-concept develops from how we imagine others see and judge us.

This chapter explains socialization as the lifelong process through which people learn to become competent members of society by internalizing norms, values, beliefs, and expected behaviors. It opens with Noel’s experience in a hospital to show that socialization also happens in organizations: workplace culture shapes how people should communicate, make decisions, and behave, and both employees and institutions share responsibility for adjustment.

The chapter first reviews theories of self-development. Psychological theorists such as Freud, Erikson, Piaget, and Harlow emphasize early development, stages, cognition, and the emotional importance of attachment and social contact. Sociological theorists focus on how the self emerges through interaction: Cooley’s “looking glass self” shows that people form self-concepts based on how they think others see them, while Mead argues that children develop the self by learning to take the role of others, progressing through the preparatory, play, and game stages and eventually understanding the generalized other. The chapter also presents Kohlberg’s stages of moral development—preconventional, conventional, and postconventional—and discusses Gilligan’s critique that morality may be shaped by gender socialization, though her findings were not supported by later research. A key theme is the difference between psychology, which looks mainly at mental processes, and sociology, which emphasizes social structures, institutions, and interactions.

Next, the chapter explains why socialization matters. It is essential for society because it transmits culture from one generation to the next, allowing society to continue. It is essential for individuals because it gives people language, identity, and the skills needed to function in daily life. The chapter situates this within the nature-versus-nurture debate, noting that both genetics and social environment influence behavior. Examples such as identical twins raised apart and Chris Langan’s life show that intelligence alone does not guarantee success; socialization also provides practical intelligence, communication skills, and familiarity with institutions. The chapter also shows how major sociological perspectives view socialization: functionalists see it as necessary for social order and cultural continuity, conflict theorists see it as a way inequality is reproduced across generations, and interactionists focus on everyday symbolic messages, such as gendered clothing.

The chapter then identifies major agents of socialization. Family is the first and most influential, teaching children how to use objects, relate to others, and understand the world. Family socialization is shaped by social class, race, religion, historical period, and gender norms; for example, higher-class parents often emphasize creativity and initiative, while lower-class parents may stress obedience and conformity. Peer groups become increasingly important, especially during adolescence, as they help young people develop independence and identities separate from parents. Schools socialize children not only through formal instruction but also through the hidden curriculum: punctuality, cooperation, competition, hierarchy, waiting, and respect for rules. Schools also teach citizenship and national identity, though textbooks and curricula can be politically controversial. Workplaces socialize adults into organizational culture, material practices, and informal rules, and successful onboarding depends on both employee adaptation and institutional support. Religion socializes members into religious practices, symbols, and moral expectations, often reinforcing gender roles and family norms. Government socializes people into age-based roles and legal categories such as adult, senior, taxpayer, or potential military service member. Mass media also shapes socialization by spreading norms, values, and images of how people should look and act; the chapter highlights concerns about “princess culture” and the ways media can reinforce gender stereotypes, while also noting that media portrayals are changing.

Finally, the chapter emphasizes that socialization continues across the life course. People encounter age-related transitions such as starting school, graduating, entering the workforce, marrying, becoming parents, and retiring, and each transition requires learning new expectations. These transitions vary by culture and historical period, as shown by differences in college timing, child labor, military service, and delayed adulthood among Millennials. The chapter introduces anticipatory socialization, in which people prepare for future roles before entering them, such as future spouses, parents, or retirees. It also explains resocialization, the process of unlearning old behaviors and adopting new ones, often in total institutions like prisons, the military, convents, boarding schools, or some senior care settings. Resocialization typically involves a degradation ceremony, in which old identities and belongings are stripped away, followed by the adoption of a new identity and rules. The military example shows how people are trained to conform, build group identity, and internalize discipline; similarly, some organizational training programs aim to replace old habits with new ones.

This chapter introduces the role of statistics in everyday life and explains why statistical literacy matters. Statistics appear in news reports, television, the internet, and many decision-making situations such as buying a house, managing a budget, and working in fields like economics, business, psychology, education, biology, law, computer science, police science, and early childhood development.

The chapter emphasizes that much of the information we encounter is sample-based, so statistical methods help us evaluate claims and make the best educated guess from incomplete information. It also begins building the foundations of probability and statistics by introducing important terms, showing how the two subjects work together, and explaining how data are collected. A key goal is to distinguish good data from bad data.

By the end of the chapter, students should be able to recognize and differentiate key terms, apply different sampling methods to collect data, and create and interpret frequency tables.

This chapter introduces **discrete random variables** and their **probability distributions**. A discrete random variable is a variable whose possible outcomes are **countable** values, such as the number of heads in coin tosses or the number of times a baby wakes a parent during the night. Random variables are typically written with an **uppercase letter** like \(X\), while specific values are written with a **lowercase letter** like \(x\).

The chapter emphasizes that a **discrete probability distribution function (PDF)** must satisfy two conditions:
1. Every probability must be between **0 and 1**, inclusive.
2. The probabilities must add up to **1**.

A probability distribution table lists each possible value of \(x\) and its probability \(P(x)\). Examples show how to build such tables from observed frequencies or given percentages, such as the number of times newborn crying wakes a mother or how often Nancy attends class each week. In each case, the possible values of the random variable are identified, and the corresponding probabilities are arranged in a PDF table.

The chapter also introduces the idea of using class data or repeated trials to think about which values occur most often and how relative frequency relates to probability. This foundation prepares students to work with and classify discrete probability models.

By the end of the chapter, students should be able to:
- recognize and interpret discrete probability distribution functions,
- calculate and interpret expected values,
- recognize and apply the **binomial**, **Poisson**, **geometric**, and **hypergeometric** distributions,
- and classify word problems according to the correct discrete distribution.

This chapter explains how the Atlantic World emerged from older patterns of trade, conquest, and migration. As Europeans sought Asian luxuries such as spices, silk, and porcelain, they looked for cheaper sea routes after overland trade through the Silk Road became more dangerous and costly. That search led them to encounter the Americas and to draw West Africa into a new transatlantic system shaped by commerce, conquest, and slavery.

In the Americas, the first peoples likely migrated from Asia across Beringia between about 15,000 and 9,000 years ago, then spread throughout North and South America. Around 10,000 years ago, agriculture and animal domestication increased food supplies, encouraging settled life and the growth of complex societies. In Mesoamerica, civilizations shared features such as polytheism, blood sacrifice, maize-based agriculture, mathematics, calendars, large ceremonial architecture, long-distance trade, and the region’s only known written languages. The Olmec, flourishing on Mexico’s Gulf Coast, laid the foundations for later Mesoamerican cultures with their art, irrigation, trade networks, and religious traditions. Teotihuacan became a major urban and trade center, while the Maya developed city-states, perfected calendars and writing, created mathematical systems, and built temples and observatories before declining after drought and poor soils; Spanish conquest later destroyed many surviving codices. The Aztec, or Mexica, built Tenochtitlán on Lake Texcoco into a vast, highly organized capital with markets, aqueducts, chinampas, and daily ritual human sacrifice tied to their understanding of cosmic balance and divine power. In South America, the Inca created a vast Andean empire linked by roads, relay runners, and quipu record keeping. Their society depended on state labor demands such as the mita, terrace farming, storage systems, and a powerful ruling class centered on the sun god Inti; human sacrifice was rare but used in emergencies. Machu Picchu stands as a notable ceremonial Incan city built with extraordinary stonework. North of these empires, Native peoples were more dispersed and generally less centralized, though some societies such as the Pueblo, Hopewell, and Cahokia developed significant agricultural, architectural, artistic, and trading traditions. Gender roles in many eastern tribes were more complementary and often matrilineal than in Europe, and Native conceptions of land emphasized shared use rather than private ownership, creating a major source of conflict with Europeans.

Europe on the Brink of Change describes the medieval world that produced the explorers. After Rome’s fall, Europe was fragmented, rural, and feudal: lords owned land, knights provided military service, and serfs worked the land in exchange for protection. Daily life was hard, short, and shaped by the agricultural calendar. The Catholic Church remained the most powerful unifying institution in western Europe, especially after the Great Schism separated the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches. The Church controlled education, interpreted scripture, administered sacraments, and could excommunicate rulers. Christianity framed the world in spiritual terms, teaching that God and Satan battled for human souls. Islam, arising in the seventh century with Muhammad’s revelations, rapidly expanded across the Middle East, North Africa, and into Spain. Christian and Muslim conflict shaped the Battle of Tours, the Reconquista, and the Crusades. Jerusalem’s sacred significance to Jews, Christians, and Muslims made it a focal point of religious war. Although the Crusades were brutally violent and intensified anti-Jewish and anti-Muslim persecution, they also expanded trade and exposed Europeans to eastern goods. The demand for Asian products encouraged merchants to seek faster sea routes. Portugal, under Prince Henry the Navigator, pioneered Atlantic exploration with caravels and navigation tools, while Spain unified under Ferdinand and Isabella, who also launched the Inquisition. European exploration was driven by “God, glory, and gold”: missionary zeal, hopes for prestige and territory, and the desire for wealth. Marco Polo’s travel account fed these ambitions. In 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella ended Muslim rule in Granada, expelled unconverted Jews, and sponsored Columbus, who sailed west and reached the Bahamas, mistakenly believing he had found Asia.

West Africa and the Role of Slavery shows that the Atlantic slave trade built on older African, Islamic, and European systems of bondage. West Africa’s varied environments supported farming, herding, and trade along major rivers such as the Senegal, Gambia, Niger, Volta, and Congo. Most people lived in small clan-based villages, practiced polygyny, and spoke many languages. Islam spread into West Africa through trade and conquest, bringing political and legal structures and converting some rulers. The Ghana Empire grew rich by taxing trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt, while Mali replaced Ghana under Sundiata Keita and flourished under Muslim administration; Mansa Musa’s pilgrimage to Mecca displayed Mali’s wealth. Timbuktu became a major center of Islamic learning and commerce, including the slave trade, and Songhay later eclipsed Mali.

Slavery itself long predated European colonization. In Africa and elsewhere it could arise through war, famine, debt, or dependency, and in many cases enslaved people were absorbed into households or tribes. Arab and Muslim slave trading expanded after Islam’s rise, enslaving Africans and Europeans alike. The transatlantic slave trade began when Portugal sought routes around Africa and established plantations using enslaved labor, first in Atlantic islands and later in the Americas. New World plantation economies, especially sugar, tobacco, rice, indigo, coffee, and cotton, required a permanent labor force, and Africans became the preferred workers because of the existing African slave trade, their agricultural skills, and the racial identification made possible by skin color. Europeans initially tried to enslave Native peoples, but disease and harsh treatment decimated them. As a result, slavery in the Americas became hereditary and increasingly race-based, unlike many older forms of bondage in Africa and Europe. Indentured servants in English colonies temporarily filled labor needs, but the expansion of plantation agriculture made African slavery central to the Atlantic World and laid the foundation for race-based slavery in the New World.

The chapter explains how the Atlantic World emerged through European exploration, conquest, colonization, religious conflict, and exchange with the Americas. Portuguese explorers, supported by Prince Henry the Navigator, built an Atlantic trading empire through island colonies, African coastal forts such as Elmina, and trade routes extending to Africa, Asia, and Brazil. Their contact with West Africa intensified the Atlantic slave trade, especially as enslaved Africans were used to produce sugar on Atlantic islands, creating a plantation model that later spread across the Americas. Spain then surpassed Portugal, unifying under Ferdinand and Isabella, completing the Reconquista in 1492, and sponsoring Columbus’s westward voyage in search of Asia, wealth, and Christian expansion. Columbus’s landing in the Caribbean launched Spanish empire-building, though his “discovery” was shaped by misinformation, self-promotion, and the eventual realization—through explorers like Amerigo Vespucci—that the lands were a new continent, later named America.

Spanish conquest depended not only on military force but also on Indigenous politics, alliances, and disease. Hernán Cortés conquered the Aztec Empire by exploiting divisions among Native peoples, especially through alliances with the Tlaxcalan, while smallpox devastated Tenochtitlán and helped bring about its fall in 1521. Malintzin (La Malinche) served as an essential translator and intermediary, showing that Native peoples actively shaped conquest. Francisco Pizarro later toppled the Inca Empire and founded Lima, while other expeditions led by de Soto and Coronado searched fruitlessly for gold in North America. The chapter also emphasizes that Spanish silver and gold helped fuel Spain’s Siglo de Oro, a cultural “Golden Age” that supported major achievements in literature and art.

Religious upheaval transformed the Atlantic World as the Protestant Reformation challenged Catholic unity. Martin Luther attacked indulgences, church taxes, and Latin-only worship, helping launch Lutheranism. John Calvin built a stricter theology centered on predestination and scripture, and Calvinism spread widely. In England, Henry VIII broke with Rome to secure an annulment and a male heir, creating the Church of England. Later conflict over religion continued under Mary I and Elizabeth I, while Puritans sought further reform and many eventually migrated to New England. These religious divisions fueled war, especially between Catholic Spain and Protestant England and the Dutch Republic. Spain’s Armada was defeated in 1588, marking a turning point in imperial rivalry. Violence also erupted in France, as shown by the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre.

Spain’s supremacy was increasingly challenged by England, France, and the Dutch. English expansion began slowly due to domestic instability and lack of capital, but England still asserted claims through John Cabot, privateering against Spanish shipping, and failed early colonies such as Roanoke. The first permanent English colony, Jamestown, survived despite starvation, disease, and conflict with Native peoples. English colonization soon expanded to the Caribbean and New England: Barbados and other islands became commercial sugar colonies dependent on enslaved labor, while Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay were founded by Puritan settlers seeking religious refuge. French colonization began with Jacques Cartier, then advanced under Samuel de Champlain, who founded Quebec and built alliances with Native peoples, especially the Huron and Algonquins, to support the fur trade. The French also established sugar colonies in the Caribbean. The Dutch entered the Atlantic as a commercial power through the Dutch West India Company, founding New Netherland and developing fur trade networks around New Amsterdam and Fort Orange, while also expanding in the Caribbean.

Labor systems, commerce, and the Columbian Exchange reshaped the Americas. Because European settlers were too few to supply labor, Spain used the encomienda system to compel Native labor under the guise of Christian duty, but in practice this led to harsh exploitation and widespread violence. Bartolomé de Las Casas condemned these abuses, helping inspire the New Laws and the “Black Legend,” which depicted Spain as uniquely cruel and was used by rival Europeans to justify their own colonization. Yet all European powers participated in Native dispossession and exploitation. Africans became another major labor force in the Americas, especially on sugar plantations, where enslaved people endured brutal conditions producing sugar, molasses, and rum. Mercantilism guided European colonial economies: colonies were to supply raw materials and precious metals to the mother country, while buying finished goods only from it. At the same time, Native goods were commodified for European markets, turning items like silver, tobacco, cacao, and chicha into commercial products. The Columbian Exchange carried plants, animals, and microbes across the Atlantic: sugar and tobacco became major global cash crops; chocolate was introduced from Mesoamerica to Europe; and Old World animals such as horses, pigs, cattle, and chickens transformed American environments. Most devastatingly, Europeans introduced diseases like smallpox, measles, and chickenpox, which caused catastrophic Native population loss and profound social disruption, including intensified mourning wars in eastern North America.

The eighteenth century was the era in which Great Britain emerged as a major commercial and military empire and its North American colonies expanded dramatically. By 1750, over a million British migrants and enslaved Africans lived along the Atlantic seaboard, and most Anglo-American colonists saw themselves as loyal British subjects in politics, religion, race, and culture.

Under Charles II after the Restoration of 1660, England strengthened its empire by creating the Restoration colonies of New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the Carolinas, all initially proprietary colonies. The Carolinas developed into a plantation region shaped by migrants from Barbados, slavery, and export agriculture: the South grew rice and indigo, while the North produced naval stores, tobacco, and deerskins. South Carolina quickly became majority Black, and slave laws modeled on the Barbados codes hardened racial slavery. Native peoples in the region were disrupted by disease, trade dependency, land encroachment, and kidnapping by traders, leading to the Yamasee War, a major Native coalition effort to expel the English.

In New York and New Jersey, England seized New Netherland from the Dutch amid Anglo-Dutch rivalry. English rule brought large estates, a representative assembly, and a diverse urban population in New York City, including many religions and enslaved people. The Iroquois Five Nations pursued neutrality between the English and French, preserving autonomy while benefiting from trade. Pennsylvania, granted to William Penn to settle a royal debt, became a Quaker haven founded on religious tolerance, pacifism, fair dealings with Native peoples, and relatively low levels of frontier war in its early years. Philadelphia became a major port and center of Atlantic commerce, migration, print culture, and the slave trade.

To regulate imperial trade, England used mercantilist Navigation Acts, which restricted shipping, listed “enumerated articles” such as sugar, tobacco, rice, and molasses, and aimed to channel colonial commerce through England. Enforcement was often weak because of “salutary neglect” under Robert Walpole, encouraging smuggling, especially in New England.

The Glorious Revolution of 1688–1689 overthrew James II, whose Catholicism, centralizing policies, standing army, and imitation of Louis XIV alarmed Protestants. In the colonies, the Dominion of New England, ruled by Edmund Andros, intensified resentment by threatening land titles and trade freedoms. After William and Mary took the throne, the 1689 Bill of Rights established constitutional monarchy, Parliament’s supremacy, trial by jury, and habeas corpus. John Locke’s political theory argued that government rested on a contract to protect life, liberty, and property. The Toleration Act of 1689 expanded freedom for many Protestant dissenters but excluded Catholics; several colonies also resisted establishing an official church.

Slavery became a central institution of the British Empire and shaped labor, economy, and racial ideology in all colonies. The Royal African Company monopolized the slave trade until 1689, transporting vast numbers of Africans across the Middle Passage. Enslaved Africans formed families and communities, preserved cultural practices, and resisted through everyday defiance, escape, and maroon communities. Major resistance included the Stono Rebellion of 1739 in South Carolina, led by Jemmy, after which the colony passed the harsh Negro Act of 1740 to limit movement, assembly, literacy, and self-provisioning. In New York City in 1741, fires triggered panic and rumors of a slave conspiracy; authorities arrested hundreds, executed seventeen people, and sold many others, even though evidence for an actual plot was weak. These events revealed the depth of white fear and the brutality of racial control.

The growth of slavery and servitude helped create a wealthy colonial gentry, especially in the Chesapeake. Genteel elites modeled themselves on the English aristocracy through large houses, refinement, and conspicuous consumption. William Byrd II’s diary shows both elite learning and the casual cruelty of slaveholding life. A broader consumer revolution connected colonists more closely to Britain through imported goods, tea culture, books, pamphlets, newspapers, magazines, and novels. Printed works such as Cato’s Letters and The Spectator spread Whig ideas, liberty-consciousness, and standards of polite conduct, while novels also opened new intellectual space for some women readers.

The First Great Awakening was an emotional Protestant revival movement that swept the British Atlantic in the eighteenth century. New Light preachers rejected formal worship in favor of personal conversion and heartfelt religion, appealing especially to women, the young, and the lower ranks. The movement produced controversy and division between New Lights and Old Lights. Key figures included Theodorus Frelinghuysen, Gilbert Tennent, Jonathan Edwards, and George Whitefield. The revival encouraged new denominations such as Baptists, Methodists, and Presbyterians, weakened older church establishments, and created a shared transatlantic religious experience.

The Enlightenment, by contrast, emphasized reason, science, and toleration. Its core ideas included rationalism, empiricism, progress, and cosmopolitanism. Freemasonry spread these ideals in a fraternal setting, and Benjamin Franklin embodied Enlightenment values in British America through print culture, civic projects, scientific experimentation, and practical self-improvement. His deism stressed morality over doctrine and informed institutions such as the Library Company of Philadelphia, the American Philosophical Society, the University of Pennsylvania, and Pennsylvania Hospital. His work on electricity and lightning rods showed the practical power of observation and reason. Georgia, founded by James Oglethorpe in 1732 as a buffer against Spanish Florida and a refuge for the “worthy poor,” reflected Enlightenment reform ideals, including land distribution, hard work, and initially bans on alcohol and slavery; yet by the 1750s, slavery had been introduced and rice cultivation expanded.

Finally, the chapter traces a series of imperial wars that tied Britain and its colonies together while reshaping Native alliances. King William’s War and Queen Anne’s War were indecisive struggles with France; the latter included the Deerfield raid and Eunice Williams’s captivity and adoption into Mohawk life. The War of Jenkins’ Ear centered on British-Spanish rivalry and Georgia’s strategic position. King George’s War briefly brought British gains such as Louisbourg, but the decisive conflict was the French and Indian War. It began over the Ohio Valley, where Virginian planters and the Ohio Company sought western land while France built Fort Duquesne. Early British defeats included Washington’s surrender at Fort Necessity and Braddock’s disastrous campaign. The tide turned when William Pitt invested heavily in the war, colonial recruits were encouraged, and Native allies shifted through the Treaty of Easton. Britain captured Quebec and Montreal, and the Treaty of Paris in 1763 ended New France and made Britain the dominant global empire, gaining territory in North America, the West Indies, Africa, and India. Although colonists celebrated their shared British identity, the war also left Britain deeply in debt and set the stage for the imperial reforms and colonial tensions that would soon threaten the empire’s unity.

By the 1830s, the northeastern United States had undergone an industrial and market revolution that reshaped work, consumption, transportation, and social life. Manufacturing shifted from skilled artisan production to centralized factory production, first through the putting-out system and then through water-powered textile mills pioneered by Samuel Slater and later expanded by Francis Cabot Lowell and the Boston Associates. In these mills, production became mechanized, specialized, repetitive, and deskilled, and workers—first often young women from New England farm families—labored under strict discipline in company towns such as Lowell. Although factory work created wage opportunities and increased output dramatically, it also brought low pay, long hours, dangerous conditions, abuse, and loss of autonomy. Workers responded with strikes and early labor organization, including the Lowell Factory Girls Association and the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association. Critics argued that industrial capitalism concentrated wealth unfairly, leading to the labor theory of value and political agitation by groups like the Working Men’s Party, which called for radical equality, an end to imprisonment for debt, and broader voting and property rights.

Industrialization also transformed consumption and daily life. Mass production made goods once considered luxuries—oil lamps, stoves, carpets, wallpaper, clocks, and upholstered furniture—widely available, while factory work changed the rhythm of labor and family life. At the same time, the rise of wage labor and the influx of immigrants, especially German and Irish, weakened workers’ bargaining power and helped create a precarious urban working class, visible in overcrowded, poverty-stricken neighborhoods like Five Points in New York City.

The same period also saw the growth of a vibrant capitalist republic. The United States became a market economy increasingly driven by prices, credit, speculation, and booms and busts. Federal land policies and “land fever” encouraged western settlement through land offices, public auctions, and credit sales, while speculation helped fuel the Panic of 1819, the nation’s first major depression. The crash resulted from overextended banking, inflation, collapsing agricultural prices, falling demand after the Napoleonic Wars, and widespread defaults, leading to bank failures, unemployment, debt crises, and foreclosures. Congress responded by lowering land prices and easing payment terms, helping the economy recover by the early 1820s.

American entrepreneurship and invention accelerated dramatically. Eli Whitney’s cotton gin expanded cotton production and, along with his work on machine tools and interchangeable parts, influenced manufacturing. Robert Fulton’s steamboat revolutionized river transport, Cyrus McCormick’s reaper and John Deere’s plow transformed agriculture and opened the prairies, and Samuel Morse’s telegraph sped communication and helped integrate business and politics across long distances.

The transportation revolution tied these developments together. Roads such as the Cumberland Road, turnpikes, canals, and especially the Erie Canal dramatically lowered shipping costs and travel times, connected eastern cities to western markets, and made settlement and commerce more efficient. Railroads, beginning in the 1830s and expanding rapidly by midcentury, further accelerated movement of people and goods, stimulated coal, iron, and steel production, and reduced regional isolation.

These economic changes produced a new social order based on class divisions. An economic elite of merchants, bankers, and industrial capitalists consolidated wealth, social exclusivity, and political influence, often supporting slavery through ties to the cotton economy. A self-made manufacturing elite celebrated hard work and merit, while the middle class valued discipline, morality, education, cleanliness, and domestic respectability; middle-class women managed households and consumption, and many middle-class men and women were active in temperance and anti-slavery reform. The working class, meanwhile, lived in unstable conditions, often relied on women’s and children’s labor or home piecework, and developed its own neighborhood culture of taverns, entertainment, and popular amusements such as P. T. Barnum’s shows. Class attitudes also shaped views on slavery: elites were often ambivalent or supportive, middle-class reformers were more likely to oppose it, and many workers feared abolition because it might increase labor competition.

The chapter examines the political turmoil of the Gilded Age, a period marked by corruption, weak national leadership, and growing public frustration with the federal government. Mark Twain’s phrase “Gilded Age” captured the era’s surface prosperity and industrial growth, which masked deep inequality and widespread graft. National politics after Reconstruction were dominated by closely contested elections, presidents who won the Electoral College without popular majorities, and a Congress heavily influenced by patronage and business interests. The disputed election of 1876 set the tone: Rutherford B. Hayes became president through the Compromise of 1877, which ended federal Reconstruction in the South in exchange for Democratic acceptance of his victory. This deal restored “home rule” to southern Democrats but was widely condemned, especially by African Americans, as a betrayal.

Three major political issues shaped the era: patronage, tariffs, and currency. The spoils system kept government jobs tied to party loyalty rather than merit, encouraging inefficiency and corruption. Reformers pushed civil service reform, leading to the Pendleton Civil Service Act of 1883 after President James A. Garfield was assassinated by Charles Guiteau, a disappointed office seeker. The law created a merit-based system for some federal jobs and limited the ability of presidents to expand patronage. Tariffs also divided the nation: manufacturers favored high protective tariffs, while farmers and consumers wanted lower rates. Monetary policy was another major conflict. Business interests generally supported the gold standard, which limited the money supply and favored creditors, while farmers and workers wanted free coinage of silver or a bimetallic system to increase currency, raise prices, and ease debt.

Farmers faced severe economic hardship in the late nineteenth century. Overproduction, declining crop prices, railroad freight rates, high tariffs on manufactured goods, and tight credit pushed many into debt. In response, farmers organized first through the Grange, which promoted cooperatives and helped inspire state-level Granger Laws regulating railroads and grain elevators. Later, the Farmers’ Alliance broadened the movement, uniting White and Black farmers and including many women. It advocated railroad regulation, inflationary monetary policy, and the subtreasury plan, which would let farmers store crops in government warehouses and borrow against them. When these reforms failed to gain support, the movement entered electoral politics through the Populist Party, or People’s Party, founded in 1891. The Populists’ Omaha Platform called for railroad regulation, direct election of senators, a federal income tax, an end to the national bank system, and other reforms aimed at strengthening government action on behalf of ordinary people.

The economic collapse of the Depression of 1893 widened the appeal of Populist ideas. Railroad speculation, bank failures, and industrial collapse produced massive unemployment, homelessness, and labor unrest. Relief efforts such as Coxey’s Army, which marched on Washington to demand public works jobs, were ignored. The Pullman Strike of 1894, led by Eugene V. Debs, further revealed the power of railroad labor and the government’s willingness to use federal troops and court injunctions against workers. These events made the Populists’ critique of government inaction more persuasive to farmers and industrial workers alike.

The 1896 election became the high point and turning point of Populism. Republicans nominated William McKinley, who supported the gold standard and protective tariffs. Democrats nominated William Jennings Bryan, who championed free silver and spoke for farmers and workers in his famous “Cross of Gold” speech. The Populists endorsed Bryan as well, hoping to build a broad reform coalition. Bryan’s campaign energized many voters, but McKinley won the election, restored Republican strength, and helped end the Populists’ rise as an independent third party. Populism declined for several reasons: the Democratic fusion damaged its separate identity, the Klondike Gold Rush eased pressure on the gold standard by expanding the money supply, and the Spanish-American War stimulated the economy and farm demand. Even so, the Populist movement left a lasting legacy by introducing reforms and ideas that would later reappear in Progressive Era politics.
